newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU mulls industrial goods deal for Central America.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls industrial goods deal for Central America.

text.p: The European Union said on Wednesday it would examine whether to extend existing trade instruments for farm produce to industrialised goods in a bid to help Central American states develop their war-torn economies.

"A lot has been done but we have proposed...that more can be done," European Commissioner Manuel Marin told reporters in The Hague after meeting six Central American countries within the so-called San Jose dialogue.
"We (EU) expressed our interest in strengthening and deepening economic and financial cooperation with Central America," he said.

Marin said relations between Central America and the EU had been based on traditional exports such as coffee and bananas, but in recent years new trade instruments, like the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) for farm products, had prompted some diversification of exports.
"Currently one third of Central American exports to the EU are no longer traditional products. That means these mechanisms are working.
"On behalf of the European Union I have undertaken to examine the GSP for industrial products," Marin said.
Marin did not put any timescale on his examination, but this will likely come under a general review of the GSP for industrial goods due next year.

Costa Rican External Relations Minister Fernando Naranjo welcomed the decision, saying through an interpreter: "We think it is absolutely essential and would be very important for enhancing the integration of our products in European markets.
"It would also be important to ensure a higher flow of investment from the European Union to Central America."
Marin said any extension of the GSP would involve a transfer from traditional farm products to processed industrial goods with much higher added value, linked to European investment.
Last year, the Central American states of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama had a combined $500 million trade surplus with the EU.
Marin, however, noted two weaknesses that needed action.
Firstly, the low level of direct European investment in the region versus the rest of Latin America and, secondly, how to get Europeans to support small, under-developed markets.
"We have to get our partners to understand that Central America's problem is the small size of its national markets.
"With the trend towards globalisation, it's very difficult to convince European investors to invest in very small markets."

"We shall have to look at how to establish a regional framework for Central America. We think it is vital that that has to be consolidated," he said, adding that the best way to proceed would be through joint-ventures.

The ministerial meeting also agreed to cooperate on strengthening the rule of law in Central America, promoting human rights, reforming tax systems to more fairly distribute wealth, fighting drug and arms trafficking and turning the region into an anti-personnel-mine-free area by 2000.
